text: Can teacher-guided edge removal make GNNs cheaper while preserving node-classification accuracy?
A proposal for sparse graph learning with knowledge distillation

Target: 1 minute(s).

Introduce the problem and frame this as a proposal. State that the completed evidence is currently a set of preliminary Cora baselines. Q&A follows the 20-minute talk.
Sparse graphs promise lower inference cost
The project asks how to remove edges without losing the useful message-passing structure.
A GNN aggregates information along edges. Fewer edges can reduce computation, but indiscriminate removal can erase useful neighborhood signals.
Can a teacher identify which connections matter?
Measure accuracy and inference cost at matched edge budgets.

Target: 2 minute(s).

Explain the tension: graph sparsity may lower message-passing work, while edge removal can harm node representations. State the outcome measures: test accuracy and inference latency, compared at the same retained-edge budget.
Prior work already prunes edges using learned and structural rules
This project tests teacher-loss scoring plus distillation at matched budgets.
Learns which edges and parameters to remove together. Chen et al. (2021); Unifews (2025) [1, 4].
TEDDY uses degree-based discrimination to trim edges. Seo et al. (2024) [2].
Mixture-of-graphs sparsifiers adapt edge choices by node. Zhang et al. (2025) [3].
Test teacher-loss edge scoring plus distillation at the same edge budget.

Target: 2 minute(s).

Position our method against prior work: joint edge/weight pruning [1,4], TEDDY [2], and node-adaptive sparsification [3]. The proposal tests teacher-loss edge scoring and KD at matched budgets. Feature-similarity pruning is also planned as a baseline.
EdgeTrim-KD separates edge selection from student learning
The pipeline is proposed; only the unpruned, random-pruned, and degree-pruned Cora baselines are measured so far.
Train with labels and teacher targets
Reference predictions on the original graph
Learns on fewer edges while matching teacher behavior

Target: 2 minute(s).

Walk through the intended pipeline. Teacher-guided ranking produces a sparse graph at a specified budget. The student trains on that graph, with supervision from true labels and teacher predictions. Emphasize that the proposed modules are not yet implemented or evaluated.
Two GCNs play different roles in the pipeline
Keep model capacity and the edge budget controlled so the comparison isolates pruning and distillation choices.
Input: original node features + original edges
Input: same node features + retained edges

Target: 2.5 minute(s).

Explain teacher and student roles and the control needed for a fair experiment. Current Cora baselines use the same two-layer GCN architecture. Edge scoring and soft-target transfer are proposed and need implementation.
The Cora baselines share one supervised training recipe
The planned distillation run adds teacher targets after the baseline protocol is fixed.
Best validation accuracy · patience 50 · up to 300 epochs
2  Select edges at a fixed budget
3  Train sparse student with labels + KD
L = (1 - alpha) * CE + alpha * T^2 * KL(pT || pS)

Target: 2.5 minute(s).

Describe the documented Cora baseline recipe. State that validation accuracy selects checkpoints and test labels are held for final evaluation. The proposal specifies L = (1 - alpha) * CE + alpha * T^2 * KL(pT || pS). α balances label and teacher supervision; T softens the probability targets.
Cora is the implementation check; ogbn-arxiv is the next benchmark
All three current runs use the same Cora split and a matched retained-edge count for the pruned methods.
Device details, multi-seed variability, training time and peak memory are not yet recorded.

Target: 2 minute(s).

Clarify that 10,556 and 6,258 are directed edge entries in the tensor representation of the undirected graph. The timing loop is documented in the checkpoint scripts. Hardware/device details and repeated-seed results remain to be recorded.
Degree pruning retains more Cora accuracy at the same edge count
Preliminary single-seed results · test accuracy and median forward-pass latency
Random removes about 40.7% of edge entries; degree keeps the same count for a matched-budget comparison.
Latency is noisy in this small run. Treat it as descriptive; do not claim a speedup yet.

Target: 2.5 minute(s).

Read the table and emphasize the matched edge count. Degree pruning is 1.8 percentage points below the full graph, while random pruning is 5.0 points below. Latency is a single run with repeated timings and lacks multi-seed/device-level uncertainty analysis, so avoid a speedup claim.
The current evidence supports the next experiment, not a final claim
The baseline comparison is a feasibility result on one small benchmark.
79.3% vs 76.1% test accuracy at 6,258 retained edge entries.
Both pruned runs trail the full graph
One seed and short timing runs cannot establish a reliable speedup.
A teacher-derived edge score plus student distillation may retain more accuracy at the same sparsity.

Target: 1.5 minute(s).

Keep interpretation measured: degree-based pruning beat random pruning on this Cora run at the same retained-edge count. Both are below the full graph. This motivates testing teacher guidance and distillation, but does not validate them yet.
The next milestone is a controlled EdgeTrim-KD comparison
Move from a Cora pipeline check to the main benchmark and a measured accuracy–cost curve.
Specify teacher score, edge policy and distillation loss.
Train and evaluate on ogbn-arxiv with official splits.
Add feature-similarity pruning; run seeds at matched edge budgets.
Report accuracy, latency, memory and scoring overhead.
Takeaway: current Cora baselines establish the comparison protocol; EdgeTrim-KD remains the proposed next step.

Target: 2 minute(s).

Close with the next milestone and the difference between current evidence and planned experiments. Invite questions. Suggested Q&A prompts: what should the teacher-derived edge score optimize, which sparsity budgets are practical, and how should end-to-end cost include one-time scoring?
